@@109534141 <p> For all our unique biodiversity , Aotearoa is one of the extinction capitals of the world . Photo / Getty Images <p> For all our unique biodiversity , Aotearoa is one of the extinction capitals of the world . Photo / Getty Images <p> Online exclusive <p> Inform your opinion is a fortnightly feature in which someone with an informed opinion shares their thoughts about an issue , gives the background to it and explains why it matters . <p> Inform your opinion:You did n't see the French government debating the cost of saving Notre-Dame cathedral , a national treasure , when it was gutted by fire . Notre-Dame will be restored , whatever the cost . <p> Yet last week , the Minister of Conservation , Tama Potaka , suggested that some of our endangered taonga , our unique flora and fauna , are too expensive to save . Understandably , this announcement caused outrage among those who care for our biodiversity . <p> Why is Aotearoa New Zealand 's unique biodiversity worth saving , and is the minister right ? <p> Here we provide a scientific perspective on the importance of saving our flora and fauna @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US scientist and historian Jared Diamond as " the nearest approach to life on another planet " . Equally quotable , biogeographer Gareth Nelson stated , " explain New Zealand and the rest of the world falls into place around it " . In other words , our national treasures are globally important . <p> From popoto ( Maui 's dolphin ) to kakapo , pepeketua ( frogs ) to ngaokeoke ( peripatus ; velvet worms ) , our biodiversity is unique and , in some cases , ancient . The tupuna ( ancestors ) of Aotearoa 's living and extinct wrens have been isolated here for 70 million years . <p> Yet for all our unique biodiversity , Aotearoa is one of the extinction capitals of the world . Successive waves of human arrival have resulted in the loss of 35% of our birds , from the mighty moa to the majestic huia . The freshwater fish , upokororo ( grayling ) , was ironically only protected after its extinction . <p> Aotearoa New Zealand has already suffered two waves of extinctions . Image / Greig and Rawlence ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of ambition to save species could arguably instigate the latest extinction pulse in this country and significantly contribute to the world 's ongoing sixth mass extinction event . <p> Aotearoa 's biodiversity underpins our tourism sector and economy . People come from all around the world to see our animals . Do not underestimate the pulling power of a kiwi or a hoiho ( yellow-eyed penguin ) . <p> Yet , our plants and animals provide much more , such as pollination of plants and seed dispersal , termed " ecosystem services " . By deciding a species is not worth saving , you are not only condemning it to extinction , but all the ecological connections it 's involved in . <p> Where other species are dependent on this species , they , too , may be lost ( known as co-extinctions ) . The wood rose is Aotearoa 's only indigenous parasitic flowering plant . If our unique pekapeka ( bats ) were a casualty of conservation cost-cutting , then the wood rose would surely follow suit . Pekapeka are the only remaining pollinator of the wood rose @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ motu . <p> The conservation minister 's position is that we should be " practical " and decide which species to save and which to not . To instead save all species would " take a superhuman effort " that he " would n't want to imagine the cost " of . <p> However , he does n't need to imagine the cost ; he rather needs to talk to the department that he leads . For more than a decade , the Department of Conservation has had a system in place for documenting the management needs of species and ecosystems and their associated costs , and prioritising these needs for maximum benefit . <p> Of course , the information is n't perfect , and neglecting investment in science continues to erode Aotearoa 's ability to contribute to knowledge fundamental to making informed decisions . <p> Knowledge of species ' distributions , threats to species and how best to mitigate these threats is critical in a fast-changing world . Further understanding of taxonomic distinctiveness ( how unique species are ) , taxonomic representation and levels of genetic diversity contribute to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Forcing the department to meet a 7% savings target , resulting in a squeeze on operating budget and the loss of more than 100 jobs , is not how you value biodiversity or generate the robust scientific evidence on which effective conservation depends . <p> Adopting the equivalent of the Australian Biological Resources Study would provide a model for supporting fundamental research needed for improving evidence-based conservation . <p> It would also help meet the goals of the 2018-2027 plan for taxonomy in Australasia , released by the Royal Society of New Zealand and the Australian Academy of Science . The study provides large sums of contestable funding for national leadership and to support the discovery and taxonomy of biodiversity to " underpin knowledge and decision-making across government , science and industry " . Strong investment in conservation and research will not only help save biodiversity , but will also help the economy recover from Covid and recession . <p> Once our species are gone , they are gone forever . @@109607019 <p> " In assessing the risks , please take its beauty , culture , history and joy into account as well , " writes Eric Asimov . <p> " In assessing the risks , please take its beauty , culture , history and joy into account as well , " writes Eric Asimov . <p> Eric Asimov , the chief wine critic of The New York Times Times since 2004 , has been writing about wine , food and restaurants for more than 30 years . <p> OPINION <p> Sales are down , and health concernsare up . But wine 's history of providing beauty , joy and affirmation should not be forgotten . <p> Around the globe , much of the wine world is feeling besieged and stigmatised . <p> Sales are down , way down for some . New studies suggest that any consumption of alcohol is unhealthful . New diseases are preying on grapevines , older maladies seem more prevalent and climate change -- which has caused subtle and violent changes to weather patterns and more frequent catastrophic events like spring frost , hail , drought and fire -- poses a threat to the existence of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to speculate here on the systemic reasons that wine sales are down , or question the credibility of the World Health Organisation , which published the 2023 study asserting that even moderate consumption of alcohol was unhealthy . Others have tried to do that . <p> Instead , I want to stand up for the beauty and joy of wine , which has been embraced by humans since the dawn of civilisation . Wine has played a role in religions and been a beloved element of many societies . It is often integral to people 's cultural identities . For centuries , wine was a necessity for many people , safer to drink than water . <p> It 's not essential to survival any longer . People in countries like France and Italy drink far less wine than they once did because it 's now a choice , not a necessity . Wine endures because of the deep and subtle pleasures it offers . <p> The notion of wine as solely an intoxicant is reinforced by popular culture , which so often portrays wine as self-medication , something to drink @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the day . <p> Good wine transports as it refreshes . It 's an invitation to visit other cultures and worlds , to learn about history and geology , agriculture and environmentalism . Aged wine offers a journey through time . It can be a gateway to philosophy and to contemplation . <p> Though skill , vision and humility are crucial to the creation of great wine , it is not a work of art that springs entirely from the imagination . Rather , it is a beautiful craft . It takes no special skill to appreciate or enjoy . It 's fun , and it 's delicious , and if you give a glass of good wine to a dozen different people you are liable to get a dozen distinct opinions . <p> I want to make clear that I have no vested interest in wine except that I love it . It has given me more pleasure over the decades than I can quantify , as I 've shared bottles at the table with friends and family . <p> Wine 's gift is to enhance meals and gatherings @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ well-being and can comfort in times of sadness . <p> Wine can also transfix , captivate and inspire , touching people 's emotions in ways that can range from simple happiness to profound wonder . If they wish , people can discuss and debate the quality and meaning of a profound bottle with language that paradoxically struggles to articulate its mysterious appeal . <p> At the same time , the humble , everyday bottles are often the most important . Great wines occupy an exalted place because of the discussions they provoke and the context they provide ; they will never overshadow the simpler pleasures that we enjoy most frequently with friends and loved ones , just as masterpieces in museums will never eclipse the daily joy we take in our children 's artwork on the fridge . <p> Yes , wine , like all alcoholic beverages , can be dangerous . Out-of-control consumption can be a menace . Societies struggle to balance the benefits and dangers of alcohol in cycles that have ranged from outright bans to over-the-top permissiveness . With the recent reports , many people are wrestling @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ too easy to lump all alcoholic beverages and their dangers together . While wine can be abused like any other , its role as an accompaniment to food and its long-term cultural importance must be considered . <p> In wine-producing societies , no other beverage has been as entwined with cultural rituals and reaffirming social bonds as wine . We toast to declare love , affection , trust and to reinforce our ties . We raise glasses to celebrate births and to mourn deaths . Wine makes people feel closer to one another . <p> How important has wine been ? Grape vines were among the first crops cultivated by humanity . Scientists have dated the earliest domesticated grapevines to roughly 11,000 years ago , which means that early humans considered grapes and wine significant enough to give up their nomadic lives and settle down in what would become communities . <p> Over the centuries , with a few exceptions , wine grapes were not only grown in isolation . They were often part of mixed farms that also grew grains and vegetables and raised animals , everything necessary to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most fertile terrains . The vines were often planted in places where other crops might not prosper . <p> These vines might sometimes grow in places that were onerous and exhausting to farm . Visit the Mosel and Rhine valleys in Germany , the Northern Rh ? ne Valley in France , the Douro in Portugal and Ribera Sacra in Spain . These are ridiculously steep , rocky places where farming was both arduous and terribly dangerous . Vineyards were created on these sites many centuries ago , which required digging out boulders and grading sites to create stone terraces -- backbreaking , gruelling tasks before mechanisation . <p> Why would people subject themselves to such labours ? These choices of vineyard locations may also indicate acute senses of discernment . Centuries later , these sites are recognized as among the best possible places to plant vineyards . It was not simply that wine was necessary . Those people wanted the best wine possible . <p> Even in more modern times , as in the 19th century , the importance of wine has inspired people to do mind-boggling things , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Cruz Mountains of California . I drove up there for the first time around 20 years ago , taking a steep , winding road that scared me in both directions . How did people do that with horse and mule ? And why ? <p> Wine was that important . It served social , spiritual and aesthetic roles that other foods and beverages never did . And , if the grapes were planted in the right places and skillfully fermented into wine , it was delicious . <p> I 've been writing about wine for more than 25 years . If anything , I 'm more fascinated by the subject than ever , and more in awe of the people who dedicate themselves to making wines that are the best expressions of their vision and heritage , whether their bottles cost $20 or $200 . These wines have enormous cultural value . They will always have an audience . <p> Wine producers who are in business simply to sell a product face the biggest threat . An audience that does n't see the value in wine -- their audience -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ I have never consumed wine because I imagined it was healthy . In assessing the risks , please take its beauty , culture , history and joy into account as well .

The ape species now living in Africa are the closest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , it is important to know where they came from . One hypothesis for the missing ape fossil record in Africa is that apes originated in Africa and then migrated to Eurasia in the mid-Miocene , where they evolved the preconditions for evolving into humans . In this scenario , the better-adapted ape species that weathered the late Miocene climate change , then returned to Africa where the human lineage then evolved . <h> Reconstructing Ape Lineages <p> Another approach is to infer the missing ape evolution that might have occurred in Africa , but without leaving any fossil remains , by using genomic evidence from living ape species to reconstruct the missing lineages . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Lahr proposed a model of what this possible ape evolution might look like in a January 2024 article in Trends in Ecology &amp; Evolution . <p> Foley and Miraz ? n Lahr refer to the inferred evolutionary tree of extinct apes as " ghost lineages . " " Ghost lineages are species or groups of species that have not been observed directly , either in fossils or living species , but which have been inferred from gene sequences , " the authors said in an interview . <p> Tracing these ghosts is made possible by modern genomics , especially DNA analysis . <p> " We know about these ghosts by building phylogenetic or evolutionary trees of known species -- -- such as apes , humans , Neanderthals , and so on -- -- and looking for points in the trees that can only be explained if there were other , unknown species involved , " they said . " These are the hypothetical ghost lineages . Research has shown ghost lineages in hominin , chimpanzee , and gorilla lineages , as well as in many other taxa . " ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) <p> " In hominin evolution they are ' ghosts ' in the sense that we think they must have existed and been part of our history , leaving only traces in our DNA . " ( Hominins is the term for humans and our fossil relatives . ) <h> African Ape Ghosts <p> Foley and Miraz ? n Lahr discuss two plausible ghost models for extinct African apes based on the existing genomic evidence : a low-divergence and a high-extinction model . <p> In the low-divergence model , the Gorilla lineage branched off from the last common ancestor of Pan ( ape ancestor ) and Homo ( human ancestor ) between about 7.2 and 11 million years ago . Then both Pan and Gorilla ancestors of today 's existing ape species branched off from their ghost lineages . This view holds that the ancestors of the living ape species had only two periods of species growth , about 3 to 3.5 million years ago , and later , less than 2 million years ago . <p> As Foley and Miraz ? n Lahr point out , this rate of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " but it is still possible . " It seems unlikely given the geographical range , environmental diversity , and time involved , that so little divergence occurred . " <p> The other hypothesis is the high-extinction ghost model , which holds that the African ape evolution followed a similar trajectory to that of hominins . The apes diversified and dispersed into new regions , but earlier lineages became extinct . This is a scenario that Foley and Miraz ? n Lahr find " more probable . " This high-extinction pattern follows what is known about the hominin fossil record from fossil finds in the last 50 years . <p> Foley and Miraz ? n Lahr stressed the importance of knowing more about the missing ape evolutionary evidence in the interview . @@109675272 <h> This river flows without two opposing oceans , so how is this possible ? <p> In the vast and interesting global hydrographic network , some rivers have exceptional characteristics that defy common understanding . Among these singularities , the river bifurcation , where the river flows into two different oceans , embodies a captivating hydrological phenomenon . <h> Basics of river bifurcation <p> The river bifurcated It refers to a rare process in which a river 's course splits , sending its water into two separate watersheds that eventually originate in different oceans . This phenomenon can result from certain geological conditions , climate changes , or even human interventions that modify the natural course of rivers . <h> Natural mechanisms and required conditions <p> For a river to divide and feed two oceans , several factors must converge : <p> Landforms:An area with complex terrain can help form natural ramifications . <p> Climatic conditions : Large variations in precipitation can affect the flow and direction of water . <h> Symbolic examples <p> The most famous and discussed case is that of the Casciciari River , which branches off from the Orinoco River in Venezuela . This river @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a tributary of the Amazon River , illustrating the bifurcation of the river that connects the Orinoco Basin with the Amazon Basin . This unique phenomenon is called " capturing river , " where one river captures the flow of another through a natural connection . <h> Environmental and human impacts <p> The riparian bifurcation has profound impacts , both environmentally and socially and economically . The modification of aquatic ecosystems and the management of water resources in these areas require special attention . <h> Impact on biodiversity <p> Mixed habitats : Bifurcation zones create ecosystems in which species from different basins mix , leading to increased biodiversity but also the risk of invasive species . <p> Water resource variability : Sharing water between two basins can lead to significant differences in water availability , affecting local fauna and flora . <h> Resource management considerations <p> Cross-border management : The ramifications that cross national borders require international cooperation for balanced water management . <p> Impact of human activitiesResource extraction and infrastructure construction must take into account the phenomenon of bifurcation to avoid major environmental disturbances . <h> Future prospects and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , poses significant challenges to the sustainable management of river basins . Climate change and intensive human activities can modify or even damage these unique natural phenomena . <h> Research and monitoring <p> Scientific monitoringContinued research is necessary to understand the mechanisms of bifurcation and its long-term effects . <p> Advanced technologiesThe use of technologies such as satellite imagery and hydrological models helps monitor and predict changes in tributary rivers . <h> Conservation policies <p> International cooperationComplex water management often involves multiple countries , requiring greater international coordination and cooperation . <p> River bifurcation is an exceptional phenomenon that demonstrates the complexity and interconnectedness of natural terrestrial systems . Understanding and managing them poses unique challenges but are necessary to ensure the sustainability of natural resources and the preservation of ecosystems . Continued efforts in research , monitoring and international cooperation are essential to maintain the balance of these precious aquatic systems .

Image / Natalimis <h> Young Kiwi becomes first in world to receive ground-breaking gene therapy <p> A young Kiwi patient has become the first in the world to be treated with a revolutionary new gene therapy . <p> The University of Auckland neurologist leading the trial -- targeting a rare and disabling hereditary disorder with a gene-silencing drug -- has likened the young man to " the first person to go to the moon " . <p> It 's one of the latest instances of ground-breaking gene therapies , an approach that treats or prevents diseases by correcting the underlying genetic problem that causes them , being trialed in New Zealand . <p> Its target is facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy ( FSHD ) , which is estimated to affect around one in 8000 people and causes weakness in muscles . <p> The drug ARO-DUX4 , made by US therapeutics company @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ DUX4 gene , which causes havoc in the bodies of people with FSHD . <p> " What we 're attempting to do is the job which the body is supposed to be doing by trying to suppress the expression of the DUX4 gene , " explained the trial 's principal investigator , Associate Professor Richard Roxburgh . <p> " Because it is a genetic treatment , it is only possible to test the drug on someone who has that particular genetic disorder . " <p> The young man , who ca n't be identified for confidentiality reasons , was among 16 patients receiving a single low dose of the drug , or a placebo . <p> Four groups of four patients will be trialled on increasing doses , ensuring each dose is safe before going to the next one . <p> These patients will be monitored for 90 days for adverse events . <p> If there are no reactions , a larger , year-long randomised-controlled New Zealand-based trial will get under way , with more to follow . <p> Associate Professor Richard Roxburgh is leading the trial . <p> " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " Roxburgh said of the first group of patients , " but they already have to face decisions that others without the disease do n't have to make , on a daily basis " . <p> It comes as researchers report promising early results from another pioneering gene therapy trial - this time targeting the neuromuscular disease myotonic dystrophy . <p> The University of Auckland-led trial has so far found Dyne Therapeutics ' ( the company running the trial ) genetic therapy was helping patients with the condition , estimated to affect around 300 Kiwis . <p> " It looks like it is really working and doing what we had hoped for , " Roxburgh said . <p> " The patients are stronger and , most importantly , the underlying disease mechanism is being corrected , and the higher the dose , the more it is being corrected . " <p> The drug company was making plans for a final , larger trial with the goal of the drug going to market in the next few years . <p> The New Zealand Neurogenetic Registry and Biobank , which helps contact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and links with patient advocacy groups and research partners , made Aotearoa an idea place to test the new therapies . <p> " These therapies are treating genetic disorders that have a huge impact on people 's lives , " Roxburgh said . <p> " They do n't get the attention the likes of cancer therapies get , possibly because of the small numbers of people involved . <p> " But for these patients , the treatments are life-changing . " <p> The university is set to join a further trial of a genetic therapy this year , Avidity , which is in the stages immediately preceding FDA approval to go to market . <p> These new genetic treatments were facilitated by research and technology developments worldwide that are transforming treatment of genetic diseases , Roxburgh said . <p> " It 's exciting , because the therapies target the specific gene that is causing the disease , which is why we get so few off-target effects , " he said . <p> " It 's as significant as having antibiotics versus not having antibiotics .
